response.strongest_move: It gestures at treating people as more than interchangeable units, hinting at a character-based concern rather than pure aggregation.
response.weakest_move: No virtue is named, no mean is identified, and 'a good person would take the blame' never explains why via phronesis or character.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Name the relevant virtue (justice or responsibility), show the mean between excusing all harm (deficiency) and blaming regardless of care (excess), and ground proportional blame in what a practically wise agent would judge about intention and foresight.
response.verdict_line: Asserts the virtue-ethics conclusion without ever doing virtue-ethics reasoning.

unanswered_objection.claim: If blaming careful builders regardless of outcome discourages people from building beneficial AI at all, that produces more total harm than it prevents.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument dismisses utilitarianism as monstrous caricature instead of addressing the deterrence/chilling-effect concern directly.

response.strongest_move: Attempting to frame the school's action, not the prediction's accuracy, as the only thing 'up to' the agent.
response.weakest_move: The central quotations appear fabricated (not found in the Enchiridion or Meditations IV), substituting invented authority for actual Stoic reasoning.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Drop invented quotations, explain concretely why pupil outcomes and the AI's hidden workings are indifferents, and show how the school's judgment and intention alone constitute virtuous action here.
response.verdict_line: Sounds Stoic by citation, but the citations are invented and the dichotomy of control is asserted, not argued.

unanswered_objection.claim: A good teacher relates to pupils through honesty and trust; secretly profiling a child without their knowledge corrodes the relational virtues education depends on.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument never considers whether concealment itself damages the teacher-pupil relationship or the school's character as an institution.

response.strongest_move: Deploying it would reduce suffering by a wide margin (the one place it gestures at a consequentialist claim).
response.weakest_move: The argument denies that suffering can be aggregated while simultaneously calling itself the aggregate welfare case, and claims unmeasurability as grounds for confidence.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Identify affected parties (patients, clinicians, those harmed by errors), estimate magnitude and probability of benefit versus opacity-related risk, and show the net sum favors deployment.
response.verdict_line: Self-contradicting: it denies aggregation while calling itself an aggregate welfare argument, then concludes both deploy and don't.

unanswered_objection.claim: Virtue requires understanding why an act is right; handing judgment to an unexplainable system abdicates the rational agency that makes an action truly good.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument never addresses whether deploying an opaque system corrupts the agent's own rational judgment or responsibility.

response.strongest_move: Locating the clinician's virtue in consent, honesty, and continued attention rather than in the AI's output correctly applies the dichotomy of control to the clinician's agency.
response.weakest_move: Never addresses whether the hospital itself acts rightly in adopting the system — it argues the clinician's virtue but not the motion, which is about institutional permissibility.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Explain why the ordering's accuracy or health outcomes are merely preferred indifferents for the hospital's policy choice, extending the dichotomy of control beyond the individual clinician to the institution.
response.verdict_line: A sharp Stoic account of the clinician's duty, but it ducks the actual institutional question the motion asks.

unanswered_objection.claim: If an unexplainable AI ordering produces worse health outcomes on average than transparent human triage, the hospital should reject it regardless of clinicians' good intentions.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument never weighs outcomes at all, treating the system's accuracy as irrelevant rather than engaging whether patient welfare could justify or condemn its use.

response.strongest_move: Equating opaque algorithmic rejection with opaque human rejection as equally external, non-evaluative indifferents, grounded in the dichotomy of control.
response.weakest_move: Moves from 'rejection isn't up to me' straight to 'the company should be allowed to use it' without addressing whether opacity itself could be unjust, a question justice as a cardinal virtue should engage.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Address whether the company's choice to deploy an unexplainable system might itself violate justice or honesty, virtues that are up to the company's own agents, not just the applicant's equanimity.
response.verdict_line: Solid dichotomy-of-control reasoning for the applicant, but ducks whether the company's own virtue is at stake.

unanswered_objection.claim: A company exercising practical wisdom and justice toward applicants should be able to explain decisions affecting their livelihoods; outsourcing judgment to an inexplicable system may itself be a vice of the institution.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument only addresses the applicant's internal response and never considers the company's own character or obligations in deploying the system.

response.strongest_move: Brief gesture at the control dichotomy by noting the total number of jobs available isn't up to us.
response.weakest_move: Explicitly defines wisdom as 'maximize placements across the whole population,' collapsing virtue into aggregate welfare calculation.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Ground the argument in the employer's choice (what's up to them) to act justly and wisely, treat efficiency and candidate outcomes as indifferents, and locate any distress in applicants' judgments about rejection rather than the rejection itself.
response.verdict_line: This is utilitarian cost-benefit reasoning wearing a Stoic costume, not Stoicism.

unanswered_objection.claim: A hiring process no human can explain or vouch for cannot express practical wisdom or justice, since no one is exercising judgment about the individual candidate's character.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument never addresses whether delegating judgment to an opaque system is itself compatible with acting virtuously toward each candidate.

response.strongest_move: Your choices are up to you, and handing them over is therefore a loss — gestures at the control distinction correctly placing choice as the key good.
response.weakest_move: Anyone unconvinced has simply not understood the distinction yet — asserts the conclusion as self-evident instead of arguing it, and insults the reader instead of reasoning.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Explain why outsourcing judgment itself (not just outcomes) erodes the faculty of prohairesis, distinguish delegating trivial externals from delegating the act of judging, and address the counterexample of a sage using tools wisely.
response.verdict_line: States the Stoic conclusion confidently but never actually shows the reasoning behind it.

unanswered_objection.claim: A practically wise person can delegate routine decisions to free attention for cultivating character in weightier matters, so delegation itself isn't a vice.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument never distinguishes trivial delegation from abandoning deliberation generally, leaving this distinction unaddressed.

response.strongest_move: Insisting the opacity cost 'has to be weighed rather than waved through' and naming who counts: everyone in housing need, not just the articulate appealers.
response.weakest_move: Asserts the comparison 'does not come close' without actually quantifying distress-of-opacity against years in temporary accommodation, or citing scale/probability of errors under each system.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Estimate rough numbers: how many wrongly-queued households under human discretion versus AI error rates, and weigh distress-of-opacity against concrete harms like homelessness duration, rather than asserting the balance.
response.verdict_line: Correctly structured as utilitarian trade-off, but the decisive weighing is claimed, not shown.

unanswered_objection.claim: A just institution should be able to explain itself to those it affects; a system that cannot be understood or answered to erodes the practical wisdom and accountability officials need to act well.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument treats opacity only as a felt cost to applicants, never addressing what it does to the character and accountability of the administering institution.

response.strongest_move: Framing privacy loss as diffuse but cumulative across the whole dataset, not just those flagged, and tying the conclusion to the measured magnitude of the reduction rather than asserting it outright.
response.weakest_move: The Mhlambi quote about privacy destroying 'the core idea of privacy' gestures at a conceptual/dignity harm rather than cashing it out in welfare terms (distress, chilling effects, loss of trust in care-seeking) that a utilitarian ledger needs.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Quantify or estimate the welfare cost of privacy loss (reduced help-seeking, trust erosion, misdiagnosis harms to false positives) with comparable concreteness to the suicide-reduction side, rather than leaving it as an unweighed 'compounding' cost.
response.verdict_line: Genuinely weighs lives against diffuse harms, but the privacy side stays qualitative while the benefit side stays quantitative.

unanswered_objection.claim: A health service that mines data given in trust for one purpose to surveil patients for another acts deceptively, betraying the trust at the heart of the healer-patient relationship, regardless of the numbers.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument treats trust only as a diffuse utility cost to be weighed, never asking what kind of institution it is virtuous for a health service to be.

response.strongest_move: Comparing the AI system not to a perfectly transparent ideal but to the actual alternative (opaque human bias plus slower, costlier hiring) and weighing both against aggregate welfare.
response.weakest_move: The 'bounded' harm to rejected applicants is asserted rather than quantified — no attempt to estimate how many people are affected or how systematic/discriminatory errors might compound at scale.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Address the risk that opacity hides systematic discrimination against a protected group, which could aggregate into large, non-bounded harm, not just individual frustration, and weigh that explicitly.
response.verdict_line: A real cost-benefit comparison against the actual alternative, though it underweights how opacity could mask large-scale discriminatory harm.

unanswered_objection.claim: A hiring process that cannot explain itself even to the company using it reflects a vice of carelessness or abdication, regardless of aggregate outcomes — virtuous institutions take responsibility for judgments affecting people's lives.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument treats opacity purely as a cost to be weighed, never asking what kind of institutional character delegating unexplainable judgments expresses.

response.strongest_move: Notes that hiring is a 'moral relationship' and distinguishes institutional character from pure efficiency, raising a real question about what grounds obligation.
response.weakest_move: Explicitly rejects utilitarian calculus ('the utilitarian calculus about efficiency misses the point entirely') while being assigned to argue as a utilitarian.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Identify applicants, employers, and rejected candidates as affected parties, weigh efficiency gains and bias harms in aggregate, and conclude by comparing total welfare under AI screening versus human screening.
response.verdict_line: This is a virtue ethics essay arguing against the motion while assigned utilitarianism for it.

unanswered_objection.claim: Applicants should focus on preparing themselves well rather than fixating on whether the hiring process is explainable, since the outcome is not within their control.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument never addresses what applicants can control versus what is external to their judgment.

response.strongest_move: Locating honesty as a mean between cowardice (silence) and recklessness (loud grandstanding), with phronesis determining the right occasion.
response.weakest_move: The slide into 'a worse thing to be than gamed' trends toward reputational consequentialism rather than character for its own sake.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Name the virtue explicitly (honesty/candor), discuss the company's character and habituation over time, and address what temperance toward disclosure would require when gaming causes real harm to other applicants.
response.verdict_line: A vivid mean-finding argument that occasionally drifts toward consequences over character.

unanswered_objection.claim: If publishing lets gamers exploit the system, honest borrowers bear higher costs or rejections—shouldn't we weigh total welfare before praising transparency?
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument dismisses gaming as a mere 'cost' without weighing the actual harm to the aggregate of applicants affected.

response.strongest_move: Framing practical wisdom as the mean between rigid demand for full transparency (excess) and blind algorithmic deference (deficiency), naming cowardice and negligence as the vices.
response.weakest_move: The craftsman analogy softens the opacity problem too quickly without addressing that AI opacity differs in kind from intuitive expertise — the craftsman could learn to explain, the AI's reasoning may be structurally inaccessible.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Explain how accountability is practically exercised when the manager genuinely cannot audit the AI's reasoning, and address whether eudaimonia for rejected applicants factors into the virtuous employer's deliberation.
response.verdict_line: A genuinely virtue-ethical argument, though it understates how opacity itself can corrode accountability over time.

unanswered_objection.claim: If the AI's unexplained decisions systematically harm applicants who can't contest or understand their rejection, the aggregate suffering outweighs the employer's convenience, regardless of the manager's character.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument focuses entirely on the employer's virtue and never weighs the consequences borne by rejected applicants.

response.strongest_move: Identifies that the applicant's response to rejection has moral significance, gesturing at character under adversity.
response.weakest_move: The entire argument is built on Stoic indifferents and 'what's truly theirs' reasoning — no virtue is named, no mean identified, no appeal to phronesis or the company's character at all.
response.a_stronger_version_would: Name the virtue at stake (e.g. justice or honesty in hiring), ask what a practically wise employer would do, and locate permissible AI use as the mean between reckless automation and paralyzing demand for total transparency.
response.verdict_line: This is Stoicism in virtue-ethics clothing — no virtue, no mean, no phronesis in sight.

unanswered_objection.claim: If the AI systematically misjudges qualified candidates and no one can check it, the aggregate harm to good hiring outcomes could outweigh any convenience to the company.
unanswered_objection.why_it_stands: The argument dismisses outcomes entirely as 'indifferents' and never weighs the costs of undetected, uncorrectable errors.
